On that ground he does not object to Augustine’s saying “that our sacraments have flowed from Christ’s side.” Lightfoot looks instead to the ratifying of the old covenant “by blood and water” (Hebrews 9:19), confessing that Moses himself mentions no water. Clarke catalogues the readings — Ambrose, Augustine and Chrysostom for the eucharist and baptism, others for the two covenants, Protestants for justification and sanctification — thinks nothing mystical was intended, and yet passes on the rabbinic parallel of the rock Moses smote twice, which “poured out blood at the first stroke, and water at the second” (cf. 1 Corinthians 10:4). Wesley simply marvels: strange that blood should come from a dead man, “more strange, that water also; and most strange of all, that both should come out immediately, at one time, and yet distinctly.”
35:
“And he that saw it bare record, and his record is true: and he knoweth that he saith true, that ye might believe.” The witnesses take this as the Evangelist’s solemn personal oath to what he saw. The grammatical-historical commentators identify the witness as John himself, who “in his great modesty frequently conceals himself” and “speaks of himself in the third person” (Gill, Ellicott; cf. John 1:7). Robertson stresses the perfect “he that hath seen” (ho heōrakōs) — “John the Apostle was there and saw this fact (still sees it)” — and draws the doctrinal point: “this personal witness disproves the theory of the Docetic Gnostics that Jesus did not have a real human body.” Clarke notes that John “must have been pretty near the cross to distinguish between the blood and the water,” and that the words contain an appeal, almost an oath, to the truth of his testimony. The purpose is stated: “that ye might believe.”

The witnesses dwell on the weight John lays upon this sign. He does not merely report the piercing and the blood and water; he stops to swear to it, staking his known character for truth upon it (Barnes), “that ye may believe.” The witnesses find here both the foundation of faith and a guard against error. The foundation is eyewitness fact: the Christian faith rests not on legend but on what was seen by men who were there, and John writes as one who stood by the cross and beheld the death of his Lord. The guard is against every denial of the reality of Christ’s humanity and death — the Docetic error that would make his body a phantom and his suffering a show. Against all such, John’s sworn testimony stands: he saw the spear go in, he saw the blood and water flow, and he knows that he speaks the truth. The witnesses note the pastoral aim woven through it all — that the reader, resting on this faithful witness, might believe that Jesus truly died, and so truly lives to save.

The witnesses note the earnestness with which John, usually so reticent, presses his own testimony here. He breaks his habitual self-effacement to stand forth as a sworn witness, because the death of Christ is the cornerstone of all he writes. The verse thus reminds the church that her faith is anchored in history attested by those who were present; and it invites every reader to weigh the credibility of the witness, whose only motive, as he protests, was that we might believe and so have life in the name of the One he saw die.
36:
“For these things were done, that the scripture should be fulfilled, A bone of him shall not be broken.” The grammatical-historical commentators trace the citation and its force. Lightfoot allows that the words “may have some reference” to the psalm in which God keeps all the bones of the righteous, “but they are more commonly referred by expositors to that law about the Paschal lamb” (Exodus 12:46), “for Christ is our Passover” (1 Corinthians 5:7); and he adds the rabbinic sanction, “if any one break a bone of the Passover, let him receive forty stripes,” with the further ruling that the bones and sinews and what remained of the flesh must be burned on the sixteenth day, or, should the sixteenth fall on a sabbath — as Lightfoot notes it did in the very year of the crucifixion — then on the seventeenth, “for they drive away neither the sabbath nor any holy day.” Robertson marks the quotation as a free one. Barnes states the type without hedging: “John here regards the paschal lamb as an emblem of Christ; and as in the law it was commanded that a bone of that lamb should not be broken, so, in the providence of God, it was ordered that a bone of the Saviour should not be broken.” Wesley calls the victim “an eminent type of Christ.”

Ellicott widens what the Evangelist is swearing to. The emphatic witness of the verse before “is not therefore to be confined to the one fact of the flowing of the blood and the water, but to the facts in which the fulfilment of Scripture was accomplished, and which establish the Messiahship of Jesus.” He saw what might have looked like an accidental omission, that the legs were left unbroken; he saw what might have looked like a soldier’s impulse of the moment, the thrust into the side; and in what flowed from it he read a visible proof — “but he saw, too, that these incidents were part of the divine destiny of the Messiah which the prophets had foretold.” On which text is meant, Ellicott judges the psalm “not equally apposite, as the thought there is of preservation in life,” while granting that its words “are doubtless themselves a poetic adaptation of the words of Exodus” (cf. Numbers 9:12; Psalm 34:20).

Calvin presses the logic of the figure. Moses “takes for granted that that lamb was a figure of the true and only sacrifice, by which the Church was to be redeemed” — and this is not spoiled by its being killed in memory of a deliverance already given, for while God meant it to celebrate the former favour “he also intended that it should exhibit the spiritual deliverance of the Church, which was still future.” So Paul applies the rule about eating it to Christ without hesitation, and bids us keep the feast “not with old leaven, neither with the leaven of malice and wickedness, but with the unleavened bread of sincerity and truth.” From such correspondence, Calvin says, “faith derives no ordinary advantage, for, in all the ceremonies of the Law, it beholds the salvation which has been manifested in Christ” — and the Jews are put in mind to seek in him “the substance of all those things which the Law prefigured, but did not actually accomplish.”
37:
“And again another scripture saith, They shall look on him whom they pierced.” The witnesses find in the spear-thrust the fulfilment of a second prophecy. The grammatical-historical commentators identify the citation as Zechariah 12:10: Robertson notes John’s verb “pierced” (exekentēsan) as a correct rendering of the Hebrew (cf. Revelation 1:7), differing from the Septuagint. Lightfoot and Ellicott discuss the textual form — the prophet’s “they shall look upon me whom they pierced,” the “me” being the Lord who speaks. Barnes marvels at “the wonderful providence of God, that so many scriptures were fulfilled in his death,” and “without any such design on the part of the men engaged in these scenes.”

Calvin, for the Reformed, draws out the deity implied: the Evangelist quotes it “to show that Christ is that God who formerly complained, by Zechariah, that the Jews had pierced his heart” — for the One pierced in the prophecy is the Lord himself. Wesley reads the looking two ways: those whose sins occasioned his sufferings “shall either look upon him in this world with penitential sorrow, or with terror when he cometh in the clouds of heaven” (Revelation 1:7). The witnesses thus find in the verse both a proof of prophecy and a summons. As proof, it joins the unbroken bone (v.36): the same Passion that fulfilled the passover type fulfilled also the word of Zechariah, the soldier’s spear accomplishing, without knowing it, what the prophet foretold. As summons, it sets before every reader the pierced Saviour and the two ways of looking upon him — the penitent gaze of faith that mourns for sin and finds cleansing in his wounds, or the terrified gaze of the lost when he returns in glory. The witnesses note the wonder that the very God who was pierced is the One on whom all shall look, and bid the reader look now, in faith and sorrow, that he may not look then in dread.

The witnesses press the tenderness and the warning of the prophecy together. The pierced One is to be looked upon — and how a man looks decides his destiny. To look in faith, mourning for the sins that drove the spear, is to find in those very wounds the source of pardon; to refuse that look now is to meet his gaze hereafter in judgment. The verse thus turns the historical piercing into a personal summons, bidding every reader fix his eyes on the crucified Saviour while it is yet the day of grace.
38:
“And after this Joseph of Arimathea, being a disciple of Jesus, but secretly for fear of the Jews, besought Pilate that he might take away the body of Jesus.” The witnesses dwell on the courage of the secret disciple now grown bold. The grammatical-historical commentators note that Joseph had been “a disciple… but secretly for fear of the Jews” (Robertson’s perfect kekrymmenos), one of the rulers who through cowardice had hidden his faith (cf. John 12:42–43); yet now, when even the chosen apostles had fled, he goes openly to Pilate to beg the body (Barnes; cf. Matthew 27:57). The Eastern Chrysostom suggests Joseph thought “the hatred of the Jews would be appeased by His crucifixion,” and so “went with confidence”; the Latin Bede notes that Arimathea is Ramatha, the city of Samuel.

Calvin, for the Reformed, and Wesley dwell on the change wrought in these timid men. Wesley sums it memorably: in that extremity “Joseph was no longer afraid, Nicodemus no longer ashamed,” acknowledging Christ “when even his chosen disciples forsook him.” The witnesses thus find in the verse a moving reversal. The cross, which scattered the bold, emboldened the timid: Joseph, who had hidden his discipleship for fear, now risks the rulers’ wrath and his own standing to claim the body of a condemned and crucified man. The witnesses note the providence in it — the body of Jesus, which “otherwise would have been exposed to the lawless violence of the soldiers” (Calvin), is rescued for an honourable burial by a man of rank and means, fulfilling that he should be “with the rich in his death” (Isaiah 53:9). And they find in Joseph an encouragement to every secret believer: the hour of trial that shames the fearful may be the very hour in which God brings hidden faith into the open, so that the disciple who dared not own Christ in safety confesses him in danger.

The witnesses find in Joseph’s boldness a rebuke and an encouragement. A rebuke, that one who had hidden his faith so long should need the cross to draw it out; an encouragement, that God can and does bring timid disciples to open confession in the hour of greatest danger. The verse thus holds out hope to the fearful believer that his secret faith need not remain secret forever, and that the Lord may yet make him brave where the bold have failed, to honour Christ when it costs the most.
39:
“And there came also Nicodemus, which at the first came to Jesus by night, and brought a mixture of myrrh and aloes, about an hundred pound weight.” The witnesses note the second timid disciple and his lavish gift. The grammatical-historical commentators recall that Nicodemus is mentioned only by John (John 3:1–2; John 7:50), and that he “at the first came to Jesus by night,” fearful — Robertson notes him “now at last taking an open stand.” He brings “myrrh and aloes,” aromatic drugs “used to preserve bodies from putrefaction” (Clarke), and in great quantity, “about an hundred pound weight” — a princely amount, fit for a king’s burial. The Eastern Cyril of Jerusalem, dwelling on the garden of the tomb, hears an echo of the Canticles — “I am come into my garden” — and of the curse rooted out where the true Vine was planted.

The witnesses dwell on the costly devotion of these two men. Calvin, for the Reformed, and the others find in the lavish spices a love that, however late in declaring itself, now spares no expense to honour the body of the Lord. The witnesses thus find in Nicodemus, with Joseph, a portrait of faith brought to the light. The man who once crept to Jesus under cover of night now comes openly, in the face of the rulers’ fury, bearing a hundred pounds of spices to embalm a crucified man. The witnesses note the irony and the grace: while the chosen twelve had fled, two members of the very council that condemned him tend his burial with royal honours. And they find in the abundance of myrrh and aloes a testimony of love — not the prudent measure of the timid, but the overflowing gift of hearts at last unafraid, which would lavish on the dead Christ what they had been too fearful to confess to the living. The night-disciple becomes, at the burial, an open mourner of his Lord.

The witnesses observe that the burial of Christ was attended, not by the apostles he had taught, but by two counsellors who had feared to own him. The reversal teaches that grace is sovereign in its timing, drawing out faith when and where it will. And the costly spices, far beyond what custom required, preach the lavishness of love set free from fear: what these men had withheld in caution they now poured out without measure, teaching the church that true devotion, once awakened, counts no gift too great for the Lord.
40:
“Then took they the body of Jesus, and wound it in linen clothes with the spices, as the manner of the Jews is to bury.” Gill follows the movement: the body taken down from the cross and carried to the place appointed for it, Joseph and Nicodemus doing the work “either themselves, or by their servants.” Robertson works over the vocabulary — the cloths are named by a late diminutive of the word used for ships’ sails; the spices by a late term drawn from fumes; and the verb rendered “to bury” covers the whole apparatus of interment, “flowers, perfumes, etc.” Clarke and Ellicott send the reader back to the earlier illustration of Jewish burial in this Gospel (cf. John 11:44; Acts 5:6).

Calvin reads the whole transaction as divine compensation. “When Christ had endured extreme ignominy on the cross, God determined that his burial should be honourable, that it might serve as a preparation for the glory of his resurrection.” The outlay was large, and “may be thought by some to be superfluous; but we ought to consider the design of God,” who “led them, by his Spirit, to render this honor to his own Son, that, by the sweet savor of his grave he might take away our dread of the cross.” Yet he will not let the scene become a precedent: “those things which are out of the ordinary course ought not to be regarded as an example.” The Evangelist says expressly that it was done after the manner of the Jews, and that manner was one of the ceremonies of the Law; the ancient people, who had no such clear statement of the resurrection and no such pledge of it as the church now has in Christ, “needed such aids to support them, that they might firmly believe and expect the coming of the Mediator.”

From that distinction Calvin turns sharply on the funerals of his own day. Those “who now bury the dead at so great an expense do not, strictly speaking, bury dead men, but rather, as far as lies in their power, draw down from heaven Christ himself, the King of life, and lay him in the tomb” — for his rising abolished those ancient ceremonies. He grants that the heathen too took great pains over their dead, and thinks the practice derived originally from the Fathers, as sacrifices were; but since no hope of the resurrection existed among them, “they were not imitators of the Fathers, but apes of them; for the promise and word of God is, as it were, the soul, which gives life to ceremonies.” Take the word away, and observance that outwardly resembles the worship of godly men “is nothing else than foolish or mad superstition.” Hence his rule for the living: sobriety and moderation, since “immoderate expense quenches the sweet savour of Christ’s resurrection.”
41:
“Now in the place where he was crucified there was a garden; and in the garden a new sepulchre, wherein was never man yet laid.” The grammatical-historical commentators first guard against a misreading. Gill takes “the place” to cover all that spot of ground on that side of the city, or the neighbourhood of the crucifixion, “for it was not a garden in which he was crucified”; Wesley says the same more shortly — “there was a garden in the same tract of land: but the cross did not stand in the garden.” Clarke supplies the custom: “it was an ancient custom for particular families to have burying places in their gardens” (2 Kings 21:18). Robertson glosses “new” as fresh and unused, and describes the place as a rock tomb hewn out of the mountain side, “a custom common with the rich then and now,” citing the royal graves set in gardens (cf. Nehemiah 3:16).

Ellicott reconciles the accounts rather than choosing between them. This Gospel makes the choice of the sepulchre turn on its nearness to the place of crucifixion, while the earlier Gospels make it turn on the fact that the tomb belonged to Joseph (cf. Matthew 27:60); but “the one account implies the other,” since the burial, under the circumstances, “required both that the sepulchre should be at hand, and that its owner should be willing that the body should be placed in it.” The phrase “a new sepulchre, wherein was never man yet laid” he reads as “an emphatic combination” of what the first and third Gospels state separately.

Calvin denies that any of it was chance. It “did not happen by accident, but by an undoubted providence of God.” With the sun near setting and the Sabbath about to begin, the mourners “looked to the convenience of the place”; and, “contrary to their intention,” they were given a grave which had never been used — “the good men are merely gratified… that they might not violate the Sabbath; but God offers them what they did not seek, that the burial of his Son might have some token to distinguish him from the rank of other men.” The situation, he adds, “served also to prove the truth of his resurrection.” Cyril of Jerusalem hears the garden answering an older song, and puts the words in the Lord’s own mouth: “I am come into My garden, My sister, My spouse” — “and what takest Thou thence? I have gathered My myrrh,” having drunk the wine mingled with myrrh, and the vinegar, after receiving which he said, It is finished. “For the mystery has been fulfilled; the things that are written have been accomplished; sins are forgiven.”
42:
“There laid they Jesus therefore because of the Jews’ preparation day; for the sepulchre was nigh at hand.” The grammatical-historical commentators explain the choice as a matter of the clock. Wesley: “they chose the rather to lay him in that sepulchre which was nigh, because it was the day before the Sabbath, which also was drawing to an end, so that they had no time to carry him far.” Gill adds the tomb’s own qualification, that it was new “and no man had been ever laid there before.” Robertson places it topographically — outside the city, near a road as the cross was, and in a garden, the hill itself looking like a skull. Clarke turns the pressure of the hour into conjecture about what was given up: from the words “it may be conjectured that they had designed to have put him in a more magnificent tomb; or, that they intended to make one expressly for himself after the passover: or, that they had designed to have put him somewhere else, but could not do it for want of time; and that they put him here because the tomb was nigh.”

Clarke draws one inference from the spices that cuts against sentiment. “It appears plainly, from embalming, etc., that none of these persons had any hope of the resurrection of Christ. They considered him as a great and eminent prophet, and treated him as such.” Yet in the burial itself he finds prophecy kept: “a remarkable prophecy was fulfilled: His death was appointed with the wicked; and with a rich man was his tomb,” following Lowth’s rendering (Isaiah 53:9); and everything attending the mock trial, the passion, the death and the burial “afforded the fullest proof of his innocence.”

Clarke then leaves the verse for the fortunes of the site, and the note has the force of a warning. The church raised over the supposed place by the Empress Helena fourteen hundred years before was, on the night of the eleventh of October 1808, “discovered to be on fire; and between five and six in the morning the burning cupola, with all the melting and boiling lead upon it, fell in.” The heat burst the marble columns that carried the gallery and the marble floor besides, with the pilasters and the figures in relief about the central chapel, until the columns themselves came down “together with the whole of the walls.” Clarke does not mourn it: “thus has perished an engine of superstition, fraud, and imposture.” What he has chiefly in view is the ceremony by which fire was said to descend from heaven every Easter-eve and kindle all the lamps and candles, drawing immense crowds of pilgrims to light a taper at the flame and to singe pieces of linen that were afterwards to serve as winding sheets — “for, says Mr. Maundrell, who was present, April 3rd, 1697, and witnessed the whole… it is the opinion of these poor people that, if they can but have the happiness to be buried in a shroud smutted with this celestial fire, it will certainly secure them from the flames of hell.”
